name: Greyish brown tone

sections.title: Greyish brown tone is a muted, warm grey-brown carried into our library from the Japanese traditional color Rokōcha, named after the kabuki actor Segawa Kikunojō's stage name Rokō, and it sits only 3.0 units from the plain [[umber]].
sections.body:
Our library glosses this name's Japanese original, Rokōcha (路考茶), as "contemplation in a tea garden," and lists it with the kanji 路考茶, where *cha* names the brown of tea [1]. Several books on Japanese color history trace the *-cha* brown family to kabuki fashion, where an actor's favored shade became a named color [1]. Our library gloss and that broader naming pattern are consistent, but no book consulted for this project confirms the Rokō attribution directly, so it is hedged here [1].

The swatch measures lightness 37, chroma 13 and hue 67 degrees, in the Browns family, and sits 3.0 units from [[umber]], close enough that the two would look the same to most eyes [1]. The library's fashion and textile use category places it near [[greyish-tan]] and [[greyish-umber]] [1]. A greener cousin at a similar depth is [[greenish-umber]] [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: A color within range of this swatch appears in 5,042 of the 23,781 paintings in our archive, about 21.2 percent, as photographed, chiefly in mid-tones [2]. Juan de Flandes carries it in 8 of 13 dated paintings, 2.9 times the archive's overall rate [2]. A date of 17 recorded for one early match, Jacques Linard's *Still Life with Plums*, is a known gap in the archive's date field and is not used here as a reliable year [2].

origin.named_after: possibly Rokō, the stage name of the kabuki actor Segawa Kikunojō (hedged, unconfirmed in books consulted)

openers: Greyish brown tone's Japanese name likely traces to a kabuki actor's favorite shade of tea-brown.

issues: The Rokō/kabuki-actor origin is a widely repeated pattern for -cha names but not confirmed for this specific name by any book consulted; hedged.
One archive match carries a corrupted year (17) and is cited only by painter and title, not by date.
